name: CERN's Large Hadron Collider shutdown explained
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person asked Claude to look up the current operational status of CERN. Claude conducted a web search and provided a detailed, factual update clarifying that CERN as an organization remains operational, but its Large Hadron Collider (LHC) was switched off on June 29, 2026, for a planned maintenance period known as "Long Shutdown 3" (LS3). Claude explained the purpose of the shutdown, its expected duration of up to four years, the scope of physical upgrades including replacement of over 1.2 kilometres of the accelerator, and the planned restart of the High-Luminosity LHC (HiLumi LHC) in 2030. Claude also provided historical context by noting this is the third such planned shutdown since the LHC opened in 2008, following similar breaks in 2013–2015 and 2018–2022. CERN itself hasn't shut down — the organization continues operating. What's shut down is the Large Hadron Collider specifically: the LHC was switched off on June 29, 2026, to begin "Long Shutdown 3" (LS3), a planned maintenance and upgrade period.

Key points:
- **This is planned, not an emergency.** CERN's official announcement states the shutdown is entirely planned and not connected to any malfunction, danger, or discovery gone wrong.
- **Purpose:** it's expected to last up to four years and will involve upgrading the accelerator complex, with the flagship project being the High-Luminosity LHC (HiLumi LHC) upgrade to dramatically improve collision rates.
- **Scale of work:** over 1.2 kilometres of the LHC are being dismantled and replaced with new systems.
- **Restart:** the High-Luminosity LHC is scheduled to start up in 2030.
- **Precedent:** this is the third extended maintenance break since the LHC opened in 2008, following similar shutdowns in 2013–2015 and 2018–2022.

So: not "CERN shut down" in the sense of the organization closing — CERN keeps running its other facilities — but its flagship collider is offline for a multi-year upgrade.

content.text: (See our AI policy here .) It’s the end of an era for particle physicists: They just said good-bye to the famed Large Hadron Collider — in its current form, anyway. The LHC, the particle collider at the European particle physics lab CERN near Geneva, shut down June 29 to prepare for the next-generation machine. The High-Luminosity LHC is scheduled to start up in 2030. Since 2010, the LHC has been accelerating protons to high energies and smashing them together inside its underground ring, which is 27 kilometers around and straddles France and Switzerland. Its most notable accomplishment is enabling the discovery of the Higgs boson, a subatomic particle that explains the origins of mass.

CERN draws up shutdown plans to save energy
Particle accelerators could be next casualty of Russia's war on Ukraine
CERN, the European Center for Nuclear Research, is preparing to idle some of its particle accelerators to save electricity, currently in short supply due to the war in Ukraine.
Serge Claudet, head of the CERN Energy Management Commission, lately told The Wall Street Journal that CERN is making plans to shut down some of its eight particle accelerators, including the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), to assure the stability of the electrical grid in Europe.
The proposal is expected to be presented to the governments of France and Switzerland by the end of the month.

content.title: Supercollider shut down until spring
content.text:
Supercollider shut down until spring

Repairs and the onset of winter will delay the restart of the world’s largest particle collider until spring, Europe's CERN particle-physics center announced Tuesday.
Image: LHC magnets
Magnets like these stretch all the way around the Large Hadron Collider's 17-mile underground ring on the French-Swiss border. Officials at CERN say a magnet meltdown led to a large helium leak, resulting in the shutdown of the collider.CERN

Scientists will have to wait until spring to use the world’s biggest particle collider for groundbreaking research because repairs to damage will run into the laboratory’s normal winter shutdown, the operators said Tuesday.

The European Organization for Nuclear Research earlier said that an electrical failure Friday, nine days after the collider was first started, released a large amount of liquid helium into the tunnel.



Experts have gone into the 17-mile (27-kilometer) circular tunnel housing the Large Hadron Collider to check on damage caused when an electrical connection between two magnets apparently melted, said James Gillies, spokesman for the organization, which is known as CERN. But they have to wait several weeks before the temperature can be raised from near absolute zero so they can actually go inside the equipment and fully assess the damage, Gillies said.

“They’re going to have to open up and really investigate what went on there,” he said. “So that’s going to be two or three weeks before we can put out something that we’re sure of.”

At least two months will be needed for the whole procedure, including the rechilling of equipment to obtain the superconducting properties needed to send subatomic particles streaming through the collider in beams that can be collided for studies, he said.
